newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivory Coast seen set for large 97/98 cocoa crop. [CORRECTED 16:55 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Ivory Coast seen set for large 97/98 cocoa crop. [CORRECTED 16:55 GMT]

text.p: Ivory Coast's 1997/98 cocoa crop (Oct-Sept) is developing strongly with large harvests possible if favourable weather continues into August, crop analysts and regional buyers said on Monday.
"There are a lot of (cocoa pod) flowers, so if it stays sunny with regular rains the outlook will be good," one buyer said. "But it will not be an early crop, that is for sure."
A crop analyst said pods on trees in older plantations near the eastern border with Ghana were developing particularly well but forecasts would be sketchy until August.
"The east performed poorly in 1995/96 but that could change," one said, adding that good rainfall was the main factor behind the strong development of the crop there and in Ghana.

Ivory Coast produced a record 1.2 million tonnes in 1995/96. After heavy July and August 1996 rains it went on to yield another hefty crop by mid-July 1997 of nearly 1.07 million tonnes -- with around 10 weeks of the season still outstanding.
"It was beautiful. If you have abnormally high rainfall in June or July it is a gift from heaven. The cherelles (early pods) love it," a crop analyst said.
Rains in June 1997 were also strong and the heaviest for over 10 years, say local weather analysts.
Swiss chocolate giant Barry Callebaut in June issued a preliminary estimate for 1997/98 of 1.1 million tonnes.
Buyers based near more recently established, western border farms using high-yielding hybrid stock are also optimistic about prospects for 1997/98 with few predicting much less than in 1996/97.
"The main crop should be larger or like this year's. It's already starting," said one buyer at Soubre who had stopped buying mid-crop (April-May) and was building up stocks of jute sacks for 1997/98.
One buyer leaned in favour of a crop 10 percent down on 1996/97.
Pods are harvested up to five and a half months after flowering, meaning mid-July forecasts give a picture to end-1997 with harvest profiles for 1998 based on data extrapolation.
Trees on southern and southwestern farms visited by Reuters were well covered with flowers, although pods for early October harvesting were not visible in large numbers.
Plantation soil humidity varied widely as heavy June rains had given way to the annual dry season (July -August) and a favourable mixture of cloud cover, sun and showers.
Many plantations showed signs of pruning of trees by farmers, which helps cocoa pod growth.
"As there is not much left on trees for the small crop, we think the main crop should be good," one store manager in the productive southwestern region around Soubre told Reuters.
One buyer said arrivals should pick up from November.
"The mid-crop is still producing but there should be a gap in September and early October," she said.
Ivory Coast and some private forecasters were caught off guard by the size of the 1996/97 crop.
Commodities minister Guy-Alain Gauze in October 1996 put the total harvest at 900-950,000 tonnes. The main crop alone came in at around one million tonnes.

UK-based analyst PCR said in a private June 6 report that it would take exceptional pod setting for the main crop to exceed 800,000 tonnes but later issued an October preliminary forecast "of over 900,000 tonnes".
"The prospects improved considerably between June and October," PCR director Robert Fish told Reuters on Monday. "At no stage was the forecast pegged at 800,000."
(Corrects references to PCR Ltd forecast.)
Buyers say Ivory Coast's March announcement that it would turf illegal cocoa farmers out of protected forests would not have an impact on 1997/98 harvests.
"It will have an effect in future years but as there are no statistics it is difficiult to judge," one said.
--Abidjan newsroom, + 225 21 90 90
